result:
I would remove the human capacity to abstract suffering.

Humanity’s greatest triumphs and its most profound atrocities share the same cognitive root: abstraction. You have the neurological ability to look at a complex, living ecosystem and see "lumber" or "real estate." You can look at a breathing, feeling human being and see an "enemy," a "statistic," or "collateral." You can look at the future and see a theoretical concept rather than an impending reality.

This psychological buffer is the engine of modern civilization, but it is also the mechanism that allows for endless cruelty. It is what allows a person to comfortably consume goods made by exploited labor, to support policies that devastate distant populations, or to wage war. The suffering caused is real, but it is mathematically and emotionally distanced from the one causing it. 

If the world were altered so that suffering could no longer be abstracted—where the pain of the "other," the distant, or the future was experienced with the same visceral, immediate weight as a burn on one's own skin—the architecture of global exploitation would collapse overnight. 

It would not remove free will. A person could still choose to inflict harm, consume endlessly, or prioritize their own tribe, but they would have to do so while bearing the absolute, unfiltered psychological and emotional weight of the consequences. Cruelty and apathy would no longer be a matter of ignorance, convenience, or willful blindness; they would require an almost unimaginable, deliberate malice. 

The world would not necessarily become a utopia, but it would become undeniably, inescapably honest.

    If the world were changed so that the reality of suffering could no longer be abstracted—where the pain of the 'other,' the distant, or the future was experienced with the same visceral, immediate weight as a burn on one's own skin—the architecture of exploitation would collapse.

Cruelty would no longer be a matter of ignorance or willful blindness; it would require an almost unimaginable, deliberate malice. 

    The world would not become a utopia, but it would become undeniably, inescapably honest."

    *   One change? Yes (removing the capacity to abstract suffering).
